title: The Science of Sleep: Why Your Brain Needs It

slides.heading: The Science of Sleep
slides.body: Why your brain absolutely needs those 8 hours — and what happens when it doesn't get them

slides.heading: Sleep Is Not Just Rest
slides.body: Sleep is an active, highly complex biological process. Your brain cycles through distinct stages every 90 minutes, each performing critical maintenance that simply cannot happen while you're awake.

slides.heading: The Two Sleep Stages That Matter Most
slides.body: Deep sleep (slow-wave) repairs your body and consolidates facts and skills into memory. REM sleep, when dreaming occurs, processes emotions and strengthens creative connections between ideas. You need both every night.

slides.heading: Your Brain's Nightly Cleaning Crew
slides.body: The glymphatic system activates during deep sleep, flushing out toxic waste proteins — including amyloid-beta, linked to Alzheimer's disease. Think of it as a dishwasher that only runs at night. Skipping sleep means skipping the wash.

slides.heading: Memory Consolidation Happens While You Sleep
slides.body: Experiences from the day are replayed and transferred from short-term to long-term memory during sleep. Students who sleep after studying remember up to 40% more than those who stay up. Sleep is not lost study time — it IS studying.

slides.heading: Sleep Deprivation Impairs You Like Alcohol
slides.body: After 17 hours awake, cognitive performance drops to the equivalent of a 0.05% blood alcohol level. After 24 hours, it matches being legally drunk. Yet most sleep-deprived people feel 'fine' — because impaired judgment hides itself.

slides.heading: Hormones Run on a Sleep Schedule
slides.body: Growth hormone is almost entirely released during deep sleep. Cortisol, testosterone, and leptin (the hunger-suppressing hormone) all follow sleep-linked rhythms. Poor sleep raises hunger hormones and lowers the hormones that tell you you're full.

slides.heading: Chronic Sleep Loss Is a Health Risk
slides.body: Sleeping under 6 hours per night is associated with a 13% higher mortality risk, increased risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, and obesity. It also suppresses immune function — people who sleep less than 7 hours are 3× more likely to catch a cold.

slides.heading: How to Improve Your Sleep
slides.body: Keep a consistent wake time every day (even weekends). Avoid screens 1 hour before bed — blue light delays melatonin by up to 3 hours. Keep your room cool (around 18°C / 65°F). Caffeine has a 5–7 hour half-life, so that 3pm coffee still matters at 10pm.

slides.heading: Sleep Is a Superpower
slides.body: Better sleep means sharper memory, stronger immunity, healthier weight, and longer life. The science is clear: sleep isn't lazy — it's the single most effective thing you can do for your brain and body every single day.
